AB Roy Chowdhury, Advocate -----For the Petitioner.

parties:
Hindu Deity Lakshmi Gobinda Jeu ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Deputy Custodian, Enemy Property (now vested property), Government of Bangladesh and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
3. Defendant No. 2, the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property Dhaka filed written statement in the suit denying the material allegations of the plaint and contended, inter alia, that the suit property is not a debutter property. It was also alleged that the suit property was the secular property of one Suresh Chandra, Roy who subsequently settled in India, following which the suit property has become enemy property by operation of law. It was also alleged that the suit property was made by the Government as an abandoned property under section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act after meeting all legal formalities and thereafter the suit property was leased out to defendant No. 4 and the lessee has been in possession thereof. 

 4. Defendant No.4 also contested the suit by filing a separate written statement denying the material allegations of the plaint and contended, inter alia, that the suit property was the secular property of Suresh Chandra Roy and he abandoned the case property without making any arrangement for payment of rent following which the Government took over possession of the suit property as an abandoned property under section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and thereafter settled the same with him and his brother Shafiuddin and since then they have been owing and possessing the same in their own right. It was further contended that the suit property is not a debutter property and the plaintiff has no right, title, interest and possession therein 

 7. Mr. AB Roy Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that the learned Courts below evidently erred in law in dismissing the suit without admitting and considering the evidence of any of the eight witnesses examined by the contending parties and on misconstruction of CS Khatian Ext. 1 and 1(a) and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decisions occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that in the face of the consistent and overwhelming evidence proving that the plaintiff Deity is the owner of the suit property and the suit property is a deb utter property and the deity has been in physical existence in the suit property all through, the learned Court of appeal below evidently erred in law, on misreading and non-reading on the materials evidence and on mere surmises, to hold that the Deity migrated to India following which the suit property has become an enemy property and subsequently vested property and the same has occasioned failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that in the face of the CS khatian Exts.1 and 1(a) clearly showing the suit property as a rent free debutter property of Deity Lakshmi Gobinda Jeu Bigraha and there being absolutely no evidence on record to prove as to how the suit property became the secular property of Suresh Chandra Roy, and the plaintiff being in continuous peaceful possession of the same all through, the learned Courts below erred in law in holding on mere surmises and conjectures that the suit property was the personal property of Suresh Chandra Roy and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate submits that in the face of the clear assertion in the plaint and in the face of clear evidence of PW 1 that for the first time on 12-5-1969 he learnt that the suit property was being treated as vested property by the defendants and that he never filed any objection in any abandoned property proceeding or vested property proceeding in connection with the suit property and there being even no suggestion by the contesting defendants to that effect, the learned Courts below were manifestly wrong in illegally finding that the plaintiff had earlier knowledge about treating the suit property as an abandoned property, as a result of which the suit is barred by limitation under section 92/(A) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and the same has occasioned failure of justice. 

 10. PW 1 Prafullah Chandra Bhattacharjee stated in his evidence that he is the Shebait of the plaintiff Deity Sree Gobinda Jeu Bigraha and the suit land belongs to the plaintiff Deity. He also stated that the usufructs of the suit properties are used for the daily seva puja of the plaintiff and for holding periodical parvans of the Deity. He also stated that the properties belong to the Deity since time immemorial as debutter property. He added that before him his father Debendra was the Shehait and before him Sharat Chandra Bhattacharjee was the Shebait of the plaintiff. He also stated that in the CS Khatian Exts.1 and 1(a) the suit land has been recorded in the name of the plaintiff a debutter property. He further stated that the original Bigraha was installed in a mud-walled temple but this temple subsequently became dilapidated following which the Deity was installed in a thatched hut and a pucca building of the deity is already under construction. He further stated besides the plaintiff Deity there are other Deities in the suit premises for a long time and the plaintiff and the other Deities were never removed to any other place at any point of time. He also stated that he sees the plaintiff in possession of the suit property from his childhood. He stated that the suit property was wrongly recorded in the SA Khatian in the name of Chandra Roy, although he had no title interest and possession therein. He stated that he cultivated a portion of the suit property himself and his bargadars cultivated the remaining portion. He clearly stated that no notice was served upon the plaintiff or upon him for treating the suit property as enemy property. He also stated that he never heard earlier that the suit property had been declared as abandoned property. He asserted that the plaintiff was never dispossessed from the suit property. He clearly stated in his evidence that he did not file any objection in the Enemy property office or Abandoned property office in connection with the suit property. He sated that Naib of Harirobi Tahsil office took his signatures on some papers on the plea that he would get the debutter property released from the list of the enemy property. 

 11. In cross-examination he admitted his signatures in Exts A and A(1), the two notices under section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. He also proved the signature of Subimal Kanti Pal in one of such notices Ext. A(3). He stated that his father Debendra Chandra Bhattacharjee and others did not file Miscellaneous Appeal No.395 before the Commissioner of Dhaka Division. 

 12. PW 2 Jogesh Chandra Dey, aged about 70 years, stated in his evidence that Kirtibashid village in at a little distance from his house and he goes to the Akhra for offering pujas. He stated that he knows PW 1 as the Shebait of the Deity. He also stated that he has seen the plaintiff Deity and other Deities in the Akhra since his childhood and none of the Deities was shifted to any other place at any point of time. In fact, these were shifted to an adjacent hut. He also stated that PW 1 is the Shebait of the Deity and he manages the suit property, as such. He further stated that before PW 1, his father possessed the suit property as the Shebait. He also stated that PW 1 became the Shebait of the Deity when his father became invalid. He clearly stated that the suit land never belonged to Chandra Roy and he never possessed it. 

 13. In cross-examination he stated that Chandra did not take away with him the Deity when he left for India. He refuted the defence suggestion that defendant No. 4 was inducted into possession in the suit property by the Additional Deputy Commissioner. 

 14. PW 3 Md Ali, aged about 59 years, stated in his evidence that he is a member of Daulatpur Union Parishad and the Akhra stands in his Union and he sees Deities in the Akhra since his childhood. He stated that the plaintiff owns and possesses the suit property through his Shebait. He stated that before PW 1 Profulla, his father Debendra was the Shebait of the Akhra and before him one. Sarat was the Shebait thereof. He clearly stated that pujas and melas are held in the Akhra. He also stated that defendant No. 4 serves in Dhaka .and he never possessed the suit land. 

 15. In cross-examination he stated that he was defeated in the last election held in 1965 by one Yunnus and defendant No. 4 canvassed for him. 

 16. PW 4 Md Amjad Ali, aged about 70 years, stated in his evidence that he sees the Deity in the Akhra since his childhood. He also stated that he cultivated some land of the Akhra as bargadar under PW 1 as the Shebait of the deity. He also stated that pujas are held in the Akhra with the usufructs of the suit property. He clearly stated that none but the deity ever possessed the suit land. He also stated that before PW 1, his father Debendra was the Shebait and defendant No. 4 never possessed the suit land. 

 17. In cross-examination he stated that he cannot say the plot No. and the Khatian No. of the land he cultivated as the bargardar of the plaintiff. 

 18. PW 5 Alauddin, an Advocate, stated in his evidence that he was appointed commissioner by the Court for holding local inspection of the suit property. After holding the said inspection he submitted his inspection report marked Ext. 3. He prepared the sketch map Ext. 4. 

 19. In cross-examination he stated that before holding local inspection he duly served notice upon the learned Advocate for defendant No. 4 but at the time of the inspection none from defendants' side remained present. 

 20. DW 1 Abdul Aziz stated in his evidence that the suit land belonged to Suresh Chandra, who was the local Zamindar. He stated that Suresh Chandra Roy left for India in 1962-63 making no arrangement for payment of rent or for the cultivation of the suit land, following which the government took over the suit property as abandoned property after meeting legal formalities. He proved notices under section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy, Act 1950, marked Exts. C to C(3) series, in which PW 1 Profullah Chandra Bhattacharjee signed. He stated that in due course of law, the Government settled the suit property with him and his brother Shafiuddin and he obtained possession of the suit land on 12-11-63 and since then they have been owning and possessing the same. He further stated that Debendra Chandra Bhattacharjee and others filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 395 of 1967 before the Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka objecting against the treating of the suit property as abandoned property. The Divisional Commissioner sent back the case on remand to the ADC (Revenue) Dhaka whereupon the ADC found that the suit property should not be declared as enemy property but the said order was subsequently set aside on review and the order of the settlement was maintained. He stated that the plaintiff Deity never possessed the suit land and the suit property was never a debutter property. 

 21. In cross-examination he stated that he is an auditor serving at Dhaka since 1967 and he lives in Dhaka. He admitted that he has no other paper except the SA Khatian to show that the suit property actually belonged to Chandra Roy. He denied the suggestion put by the plaintiff that they created false papers for illegally grabbing the suit property in collusion with some officials of the Revenue Department. He stated that he cannot say if pujas are held in the tin shed constructed by PW 1. 

 22. PW 2 stated in his evidence that defendant No. 4 has been in possession of the suit land since 12-11-67 after he was put into possession by the ADC (Revenue) he stated that the plaintiff Deity never possessed the suit land. 

 23. In cross-examination he stated that he was serving in the Revenue Department in Dhaka since 1969: He also stated that he is a co-villager of DW 1. He admitted that recently a tin-shed has been constructed in the suit land. He also stated that he cannot say how many plots are there in the suit land. 

 24. DW 3 Ramijuddin Ahmed stated in his evidence that defendant No. 4 possessed the suit land. 

 27. This case involves an element of public importance in that the same property is once treated as an abandoned property and subsequently as an enemy vested property. Once a property becomes an abandoned property, it vests in the Government and, as such, the action of the defendants in treating the suit property as an enemy property is evidently illegal and without jurisdiction in the face of their claim that it earlier had become an abandoned property under section 92( 4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In view of the plaintiffs clear case that the plaintiff for the first time on 12-5-69 learnt that the defendants were trying to treat the suit property as an enemy property and soon thereafter he filed the present suit praying for declaration of the plaintiffs title therein and for a further declaration that the defendants cannot treat the suit property as a vested property, there is no reason to hold that the suit is barred by limitation. This finding of the learned Courts below is evidently illegal and arbitrary and consequently, the same is not sustainable in law. PW Profullah Chandra Bhattacharjee in his evidence clearly stated that he never filed any objection in any abandoned property proceeding or vested property proceeding. It was never brought to his notice at the time of his cross-examination by the contesting defendants that he himself filed objection before the Revenue Authority praying for release of the suit property from the abandoned list. In the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record, it must be held that the learned Courts below were manifestly wrong in holding that the suit is barred by limitation as no objection within 90 days of the notice treating it as an abandoned property under section 92(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was taken by the plaintiff overlooking the vital fact that the whole exercise to treat the suit property as an abandoned property and subsequently enemy property and vested property is evidently an illegal and malafide move having no' touch with the reality and all these did not in any way affect the interest of the plaintiff. Moreover, from a close reading of the proceedings under section 92(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 it appears to me that the provision for institution of a suit in the civil Court within 90 days of the order of the Government treating a property as an abandoned property does not provide any penal consequence for the failure of the aggrieved party to institute the suit within 90 days and, as such, it cannot be said that the aggrieved party is debarred from challenging the order of the Government subsequently by instituting a suit. The provision of section 92(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is thus found to be merely directory and not mandatory and it does not stand as a bar against the suit as held by the learned Courts below. In this view of the matter the learned Court of appeal below erred in law in holding that the suit is barred under section 92(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. 

 28. In the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record, I am constrained to hold that the learned Courts below. seriously erred in law in dismissing the suit on non-reading and misreading of the material evidence on record and on misconstruction of the important documents in the CS Khatians Exts. 1 and 1(a) and the same has occasioned failure of justice. As the plaintiff has been able to prove its title in the suit land and continuous possession therein, I do not find any reason as to why the suit should not be decreed. In view of the fact that the suit property is a Debutter property of the Deity and there is absolutely no basis for its becoming the secular property of its former Shebait Suresh, the mere recording of the suit property in the name of Suresh in SA khatian is evidently wrong and without any foundation whatsoever and the same cannot affect the plaintiffs right, title and interest in the suit property and any way there is no dispute to the proposition that the CS khatians has a presumption of correctness undersection 103(b) of the Bengal Tenancy Act while the SA khatian has no such presumptive value. The learned Courts below thus evidently erred in law in placing too much reliance on the SA khatians completely ignoring the overwhelming evidence on record to prove that it had no legal foundation and factual basis. For the reasons stated above, I am constrained to hold that the learned Courts below were wrong in passing the impugned judgments on erroneous view of law and on illegal and irrelevant considerations and the same are liable to be set aside in the interest of justice. 

 30. The learned Courts below placed too much emphasis on Ext. 3 series showing the defendants' purported exercise of power under section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in which the signature of PW 1 Profullah Chandra Bhattacharjee, all along with others, appears. It is clear from the explanation of PW 1 Profullah Chandra Bhattacharjee that the Tahshilder concerned took his signature in the notice on the plea of releasing the suit property from the enemy property list. This evidence of PW 1 remains totally unchallenged. Moreover, mere putting a signature on a notice by PW 1, along with others, by itself does not mean that PW 1 had complete knowledge about the contents of the notice. If any authority is needed to fortify my view, we may profitably refer to the case of Amanatullah vs Ali Mohammad Bhuiyan reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 199 = 2 BLC (AD) 134. PW 1 who is evidently a man of little learning and simple manner, cannot thus be saddled with the liability of knowing the full contents of the notice so as to make this binding upon him as the Shebait of the Deity, plaintiffs.
